name: Y2K

media.title: The Matrix (1999)
media.note: set the chrome-and-latex side of the look

media.title: Paris Hilton / early reality TV era
media.note: the glam, bedazzled side of the revival's reference pool

reacts_against: 1990s grunge's deliberate dishevelment; Y2K fashion was optimistic, shiny and technology-infatuated, betting visually on a glossy future.
revivals: major 2020–present revival, amplified by TikTok and low-rise jeans' return to mainstream fashion
article: Y2K fashion is named for an anxiety it mostly ignored. The term "Y2K" originally meant the feared computer-date bug at the turn of the millennium, but the aesthetic that borrowed the name was almost entirely optimistic: it bet that the future would be shiny, digital and fun, not broken. Running roughly from 1997 to 2004, the look mixed two colour families that don't usually share a wardrobe — the cool chrome-and-cyberspace palette of The Matrix and early CGI, and the hot, glittery pinks and purples of early-2000s pop and reality-TV glamour, embodied by figures like Paris Hilton. Low-rise jeans, metallic and holographic fabric, tiny rectangular sunglasses and butterfly hair clips were the era's signature objects, all of them photographing with a slightly over-lit, flash-forward quality that digital cameras of the time produced almost by accident. The aesthetic went dormant through the 2010s, when fashion moved toward minimalism, then came back hard from 2020 on, driven substantially by TikTok and by low-rise jeans' return to stores — a revival so complete that much of what circulates as "Y2K" online now is new clothing designed to resemble the old, rather than archival pieces, which has its own effect on the palette: revival Y2K often runs a touch more saturated and color-corrected than the slightly washed-out, flash-photographed original.
